Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-10
Start time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Reyes (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (LatticePay Eng Mgr), Sam Ortiz (Backend Eng), Karen Liu (Security)

Quick hosted sandbox demo. Showed streaming, parameters, and retry playbook. Customer asked about data isolation, SOC two, and whether they should go dedicated later. Action: share pricing, sandbox repo, and sample logs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood Inference. Omar's joining from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya Nair: Good, thanks. We have Sam and Karen on as well. We're hoping to get a short hands-on so we can see how streaming works and how retries behave under slightly bursty loads.
[00:14] Omar Reyes: Perfect, we'll run through a short sandbox demo. We'll start with a quick architecture slide — apologies, deck link in chat: https://redwood.example/deck/sandbox-playbook — then jump into the console and a live curl demo.
[00:29] Sam Ortiz: Cool. Quick qual: our current stack is nodejs microservices, deployed in us-west-2, and we proxy requests through an internal api gateway. We want sub-300ms median token latency for short responses — like 80-120 tokens — and lower cost than current provider.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Great. That fits a hosted plan as long as the throughput isn't huge; we can show batching and prefix caching to drive down unit cost. If you need committed capacity we can talk dedicated later.
[00:58] Karen Liu: Security quick question — we need SOC2, SSO/SAML, and KMS for encryption. Also we have to keep logs for audit but not the actual PII — is there control over retention?
[01:10] Omar Reyes: Yes, we support SOC2-compliant environments. For hosted we have controls around retention and tokenization; for stricter rules we recommend Redwood Private (VPC) where you keep the control plane in your VPC. I'll share the security pack after.
[01:25] Priya Nair: Okay that's promising. Can you show streaming behavior and what happens if the connection drops mid-response?
[01:32] Omar Reyes: Absolutely. Live demo: I'm calling the chat endpoint with streaming enabled — using curl and then our Node SDK. Example in repo: https://github.com/redwood/sandbox-onramp.
[01:44] [screen share noise] Omar Reyes: Sending request now — prompt is a short customer support thread, model redwood-chat-medium. You should see tokens arriving in a streaming chunk every ~100-200ms depending on the model.
[02:02] Sam Ortiz: I see partial tokens — if our client times out and reopens, can we resume or do we need to re-request and risk duplicates?
[02:10] Omar Reyes: Great question. By default streams are not resumable; we recommend making streaming best-effort and having idempotency keys for the outer request. For exact-once, use our conversation API which stores msgs server-side and you can replay from a saved context.
[02:25] Maya Chen: Also, pattern is to make the generative call idempotent at your application layer — keep an event id, and if you re-request you detect duplicates. For partial responses you can show progress UI and fallback to a cached prefix if available.
[02:40] Priya Nair: About retries — what's your recommended backoff? We have bursts and occasional 429s from our current provider.
[02:48] Omar Reyes: We suggest an exponential backoff with jitter. For transient 5xx or 429, try up to 3 retries with base 200ms and exponential factor 2 — adjust to your SLOs. For streaming specifically, it's often better to return a placeholder and re-request with an idempotency token than to try replaying a stream.
[03:05] Karen Liu: And how about token accounting and cost visibility? We need per-route cost for budget owners.
[03:11] Maya Chen: Console has per-route token and cost breakdown, and Optimize will give batching/caching suggestions. We'll demo per-route dashboards in a sec.
[03:20] [Transition to console screen share] Omar Reyes: Opening console -> Projects -> Sandbox-LatticePay. Metrics show token burn, p95 latency, and cost by route. Here's a cache hit rate metric — you can tune prefix caching to reduce tokens for repeated prompts.
[03:40] Sam Ortiz: For our onboarding flow we have repeated system prompts and a customer context prefix. Sounds like prefix caching would help. Is KV cache the same as prefix cache?
[03:48] Omar Reyes: They're related. Prefix caching stores the common prompt prefix and reuses partial KV cache where supported by the runtime. We also have automatic KV cache reuse when you pin the model and keep context sizes stable.
[04:02] Priya Nair: You mentioned quantization earlier — when would that matter for us?
[04:08] Omar Reyes: Quantization helps on dedicated/private deployments to lower compute and cost — for hosted we already use optimized kernels; if you hit a cost threshold we can recommend quantized variants or smaller models along with batching suggestions.
[04:22] Maya Chen: Quick check — what are your peak concurrent users for chat?
[04:26] Priya Nair: In beta maybe 60 concurrent, then scale to ~500 QPS in production spikes.
[04:33] Omar Reyes: For that footprint we'd discuss Dedicated/GPU pool sizing. For the sandbox we'll run a small benchmark to emulate your spikes — Omar will share the benchmark spreadsheet template.
[04:45] Sam Ortiz: Can the sandbox simulate spotty network and show retry behavior?
[04:50] Omar Reyes: Yes, our local harness has a fault-injection flag. We'll include a script you can run to simulate intermittent disconnects and 429 bursts.
[05:00] [small chatter, background noise]
[05:20] Karen Liu: About data residency — we need logs stored in eu-west for some customers. Is that an option for hosted?
[05:27] Maya Chen: We have regioned hosted endpoints; we can route to eu-west and apply retention policies, but for contractual residency guarantees we typically recommend Private in that region. Details in the compliance doc.
[05:40] Priya Nair: OK. Any obvious tradeoffs between hosted and dedicate in latency and cost?
[05:45] Omar Reyes: Hosted is easiest to onboard, predictable for small-medium usage; Dedicated gives you better tail latency and lower unit cost at scale, but requires a commit and some infra setup. With Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools, and you can adjust autoscaling policies.
[05:58] Sam Ortiz: For retry semantics, does Redwood expose idempotency-key header or do we handle all that on our side?
[06:04] Omar Reyes: We accept an Idempotency-Key header and will dedupe duplicate requests that are identical within a short window — but you should also keep idempotency in app logic because dedupe windows are not a substitute for application-level dedupe for long-running or async flows.
[06:20] Maya Chen: Let's demo a failure scenario: I'll kill the stream mid-response and then show the recommended client pattern — re-request with idempotency key and show how Console flags duplicate calls in the route metrics.
[06:35] [demo noise]
[06:50] Omar Reyes: You can also enable our streaming partial-commit flag which writes a small marker to conversation state so you can resume from a last-good token in Private deployments. It's a bit more advanced and requires stateful routing.
[07:05] Priya Nair: That sounds interesting but probably heavy for early days. For now we'll stick with app-level idempotency and small backoffs.
[07:12] Maya Chen: Totally reasonable. Now quick look at generation params — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences.
[07:20] Omar Reyes: Right. Default temp 0.7 gives variability — for deterministic billing-sensitive flows we suggest temp 0.0-0.2 and top_p around 0.9. Reduce max_tokens and add stop tokens to limit runaway generations.
[07:36] Sam Ortiz: Any examples of param combos for short support replies?
[07:40] Omar Reyes: Sure — try temperature 0.2, max_tokens 120, top_p 0.9, and a stop sequence like "
User:"; also use response_length hints in the SDK to help runtime choose batching windows.
[07:52] Priya Nair: Do you surface prompt-level token estimates before we send? We want to charge product teams per-call.
[07:58] Maya Chen: Yes, SDK and console estimate token counts pre-send and post-response, and console reports per-route cost. We'll share the CSV export for billing owners.
[08:10] Karen Liu: On the security docs — can you confirm whether logs include raw prompts by default? We need to scrub PII before any long-term storage.
[08:18] Omar Reyes: By default, hosted logs store raw prompts for X days for debugging; you can configure automated scrubbers or use an API hook to obfuscate PII before forwarding to long-term retention. For strict needs, Private keeps everything in your environment.
[08:34] Priya Nair: That helps. How long will the sandbox run take and what should we instrument on our side?
[08:40] Maya Chen: We'll do a 1-week sandbox: baseline walk, run a small traffic replay from your sample logs, and do two benchmark runs with and without prefix caching. Instrument latency, token counts, error rates, and user-visible error behavior.
[08:55] Sam Ortiz: Sounds good. Can you show the Optimize suggestions now?
[09:00] Omar Reyes: Sure — clicking into Optimize -> Suggestions -> LatticePay-sandbox. Here's a recommendation: enable per-route batching for short replies with a 25ms aggregation window, enable prefix caching for the onboarding flow, and reduce model size for non-critical summarization routes. Estimated cost savings: ~27% in the suggested config.
[09:20] Priya Nair: That's a helpful number. Is that an automated suggestion or engineer-curated?
[09:25] Omar Reyes: It's a mix — heuristics plus runtime telemetry, and our Ops team reviewed the sample. We'll include the assumptions in the suggestion export.
[09:35] [brief silence as Omar pulls report]
[09:50] Maya Chen: Quick callouts: watch p95 latency if you increase batching; set a latency SLO and a per-route fallback to a cheaper model for tails.
[10:02] Priya Nair: Final question — can you share a simple troubleshooting checklist for streaming failures? Like check network->retry->fallback?
[10:10] Omar Reyes: Yes. We'll send a one-page runbook: 1) confirm idempotency key present, 2) check token/usage limits in console, 3) run fault-injection harness, 4) check model fallback policy, 5) escalate to Redwood with trace id.
[10:25] Sam Ortiz: Perfect.
[10:30] Maya Chen: Recap: We'll share pricing and reserved capacity options, sandbox repo and scripts, security/compliance pack, and schedule the sandbox kickoff. Next steps in the chat.
[10:42] Priya Nair: Thanks — we can meet for the sandbox kickoff the week of Feb 17th.
[10:48] Maya Chen: Great, I'll follow up with a calendar invite. Thanks everyone.
[10:52] Meeting end.
